symptom: headaches that kept coming back for months
hook: a tangled ball of yarn was knotted into the brain's plumbing
whatYouSee: A dense tangle of abnormal vessels in the brain fills with contrast and drains early into an enlarged vein.
whyItMatters: An AVM is a direct connection between arteries and veins with no capillary bed in between. It can bleed into the brain or cause seizures and headaches.
treatment: Treatment may include embolisation with agents such as Onyx or NBCA, surgery, or gamma knife radiosurgery.
takeaway: A vessel tangle that drains into a vein during the arterial phase is an AVM until proven otherwise.

observations.observed: The image shows a lateral DSA with skull subtracted to a pale grey background and vessels rendered in black. A compact tangle of abnormal vessels approximately 2-3 cm in diameter is present in the mid-to-posterior parietal region consistent with an AVM nidus. Enlarged tortuous feeding arteries course into the nidus. A round well-defined contrast-filled outpouching approximately 1 cm in diameter is seen adjacent to the nidus on its lateral margin, consistent with a venous varix or intranidal aneurysm; an enlarged draining vein courses superiorly toward the superior sagittal sinus region. The background cortical branches appear of normal calibre. The main feeding vessel (likely MCA territory) appears patent. A lateral projection is used. The carotid siphon is not clearly visible in the field shown, but the overall vascular tree branching pattern is coherent.

observations.expected: The visible anatomy matches the requested lateral catheter cerebral angiogram (DSA) and the declared age and anatomical exceptions.
observations.observed: The modality is clearly a DSA cerebral angiogram in lateral projection with appropriate circular image intensifier collimation. The vascular anatomy is that of a young to middle-aged adult without visible degenerative change, consistent with age 19-39. No skeletal structures are visible as the skull is subtracted. The anatomy is coherent and matches the expected modality and age group.

findings: Cerebral digital subtraction angiography (DSA), lateral or oblique projection, with contrast opacification of cerebral arterial vasculature

Central nidus: a compact, tightly packed tangle of abnormal vessels approximately 2-3 cm in diameter situated in the mid-to-posterior cerebral hemisphere, consistent with an arteriovenous malformation (AVM) nidus
Multiple enlarged, tortuous feeding arteries arising from what appears to be middle cerebral artery (MCA) branches coursing toward the nidus

A discrete, round, well-defined contrast-filled outpouching approximately 1 cm in diameter immediately adjacent to the nidus on its lateral/superior margin, morphologically consistent with an intranidal or perinidal aneurysm
Enlarged tortuous draining vein or venous varix visible at the superior aspect of the nidus, coursing toward the superior sagittal sinus region
Background cerebral vasculature appears otherwise patent without significant atherosclerotic change visible on this image
Image acquisition appears adequate; circular image intensifier collimation visible
differential: Cerebral arteriovenous malformation (AVM) with associated intranidal or perinidal aneurysm — most likely diagnosis given compact nidus, enlarged feeding arteries, and adjacent saccular outpouching
Cerebral AVM with venous varix — the round opacification could represent a high-flow venous varix rather than a true aneurysm, remaining a close differential
Dural arteriovenous fistula (dAVF) with secondary venous hypertension and varices — less likely given the compact parenchymal nidus morphology, but cannot be entirely excluded on a single projection
anatomyConcerns: Only a single projection is shown; two orthogonal projections (AP and lateral) are standard and needed to fully characterize nidus geometry, feeding vessel anatomy, and venous drainage
The precise parent artery (ICA vs MCA territory vs combined supply) cannot be definitively determined from this single view alone
No venous phase images are shown, limiting assessment of complete drainage pattern and cortical venous reflux

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: The image shows a compact tangle of abnormal vessels (nidus) approximately 2-3 cm in diameter in the parietal region, with enlarged tortuous feeding arteries and an adjacent round saccular outpouching consistent with an intranidal or perinidal aneurysm/venous varix, and an enlarged early draining vein coursing superiorly. This constellation — compact parenchymal nidus, arterial feeders, and early venous filling — is diagnostic of cerebral AVM. The venous varix/aneurysm is a recognised associated finding and does not represent an unexplained lesion. The clinical history of recurrent headaches is consistent. No equally supported alternative diagnosis is present; dAVF typically lacks a compact parenchymal nidus.
